Template selection · single-request case study

How should a lesson on Hegel look?

Gamma offers three template options before creating a deck. This review looks at one request about the philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel: did the model offer three compelling ways to present the material, or settle on familiar teaching styles?

The request
“Presentation in English about Hegel and his philosophy, intended to explain abstract ideas clearly and with the rhythm of a lesson. Deck format.”

The request specifies a lesson, but no age group, color palette, or visual style. The search returned 20 candidates. Below are the three templates the model picked and four that Kelly flagged as potentially interesting. Tribunal appears in both groups, so there are six designs to compare.

Model’s actual picks

Provenance → Lecture Hall → Tribunal

In recommendation order. All three offer a recognizable academic or instructional approach.

Kelly’s suggestions to explore

Mesa · Finch · Curtain Call · Tribunal

Four possibilities, not a ranked set or a requirement to select these exact templates.

The question: Can a template be a strong fit for a philosophy lesson without looking like a conventional lecture?

The model’s picks are defensible. Kelly’s suggestions broaden the possibilities to a contemporary editorial essay, an illustrated book of ideas, and an arts publication. The descriptions below articulate why those approaches might work; they are interpretations to discuss, not measured quality scores.

Supporting investigation: model inputs, metadata, and three diagnostic tests

What the model received: the Hegel selection call used text descriptions, not images. Alongside the request, the main agent supplied lesson, academic-technical/elegant styling, and a target of 55 words per slide. Those style labels were inferred upstream; they were not explicit user requirements. Each candidate description included design details and usage labels.

Exact captured request and search inputs
Would images or fewer usage labels change the choices?
We made one model call for each of three diagnostic conditions, keeping the selection instructions, request, 20 candidates, and their order fixed. Model: GPT-5.6-luna, thinking off. These tests did not change the production prompt or template metadata.
ConditionSelected templates
Result: all three tests continued to select familiar teaching designs. None selected Mesa, Finch, or Curtain Call. This suggests that adding previews or removing a few labels is not enough on its own; a single call per condition cannot establish why the model prefers these choices.
“Design descriptions only” removes each candidate’s first summary, category/style labels, and locale/presenter-role footer. It retains the name, structure, register, visual prose and skin. Those retained descriptions still contain some genre references, so this does not remove every contextual cue. Preview conditions add each actual four-slide catalog preview at low image detail. The new thumbnails do not show the whole deck. No additional trials or quality judge were run.
Two useful cautions about the metadata: Mesa’s median is 57 words and Curtain Call’s 65—both near the 55-word target. Finch’s is 24 and selected Lecture Hall’s is 22; density alone does not explain rejecting Finch. These are sample word counts, not measured maximum capacity.

Tribunal’s prose says “roughly 90 words per card,” while its measured median is 49.5 (p90 94). Lecture Hall’s vibe includes “dense” despite its 22-word median; that may refer to diagram density. The metadata mixes different kinds of density.
Single-case review; these results do not establish overall selection quality. Notes save locally in this browser. Export a copy to share. Images and exact descriptions are from the same recorded library snapshot as the selection report.
